title: A day of mindfulness at home
hookLine: a retreat you can keep on a free day: phone away, sit, walk, eat slowly

cards: A ten-day silent retreat can sound wonderful, and completely impossible. There's work. There are kids, or parents, or a dog who needs walking at six.
Nobody is giving you ten days off to sit in a hall. Plenty of Buddhists have been farmers and traders and parents, not monks. So the tradition keeps a smaller version too.
It fits inside an ordinary Saturday.

teach.b: One home retreat is already familiar from this path: uposatha, the moon day.
On the full and new moons, lay people could keep eight precepts for a day and a night, eat before noon, set aside entertainment, and spend the day at the temple or quietly at home.
A one-day retreat, every couple of weeks. In the twentieth century, the Vietnamese Zen teacher Thich Nhat Hanh gave the idea a modern shape.

teach.h: ONE DAY A WEEK, DONE SLOWLY.
teach.b: In his little book The Miracle of Mindfulness, he suggested setting aside one day a week as a day of mindfulness: waking, washing, making tea, sweeping, even the dishes, all done slowly and with attention.
Not special activities; ordinary things done awake. So what does a home retreat look like now?
The phone out of reach, and people told you'll be offline. A stretch of time, a morning or a half-day. A sitting, the way you've learned.
A slow walk, in a room or outside. One meal without screens or reading, tasted. One chore done as practice.
Talk kept to what's needed, a small noble silence.
This week's pieces are already here: the rains retreat, stay in one place; the retreat itself, less input, more seeing; noble silence, quiet on purpose.
A day at home puts them together on a free morning. It won't be perfect. The phone will call and the laundry will look urgent.
That's fine. Notice it, and come back.

how: Many lay Buddhists keep a day of practice at home or at the temple: in Theravada countries on uposatha moon days with eight precepts, and in communities influenced by Thich Nhat Hanh as a weekly day of mindfulness.

o: the monks' yearly ordination ceremony held at the new year
a feast day when families bring rich food to the temple
the moon day, kept with extra precepts as a day of practice

games.q: match each home retreat to where it comes from.
p: the moon day, with eight precepts
one day a week, done slowly

s: a home retreat has to last at least a week
uposatha is a single day and night, and a day of mindfulness can be a morning.
Thich Nhat Hanh suggested a weekly day of mindfulness in The Miracle of Mindfulness
he pictured ordinary tasks done slowly and with attention.
a day of mindfulness has to be full of special spiritual activities
the idea is ordinary things, like making tea or washing up, done awake.

games.q: it's your quiet half-day. an hour in, the laundry pile starts to look very urgent. what fits a day of mindfulness?
o: do the laundry slowly, as practice.
ignore it and sit with clenched teeth.
games.why: in Thich Nhat Hanh's picture, chores done with attention are the practice. the day isn't ruined; it just includes laundry.

practice: Look ahead at the next week or two for a free half-day, or even two quiet hours, a Saturday morning or a Sunday afternoon, and picture its shape: phone away, a sitting, a slow walk, a meal without a screen, one chore done carefully.
Keep the plan small enough to actually happen. Then let it go and give yourself a taste of it right here: just this breath, done slowly.

wordCard.voice: Uposatha. The observance day: a small retreat on a free day at home, phone away, sit, walk, and do ordinary things slowly and awake.

orig.note: Pali: the observance day on the moon's quarters, the oldest home retreat.

carryVoice: Your line: a retreat at home. No ten days off required. That's day one hundred fifty-four.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 8.41 (Sankhitta Uposatha Sutta), the eight-precept uposatha
